extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in comedy, cartoonists, humor writers, and participants in cartoon-caption contests
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observations about what makes things funny, with specific references to cartoon-caption contests, standup/performances, and types of comedic effect (slapstick, taboo jokes, structural devices). Useful for people creating or judging short humor pieces or captions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartoon Caption Contest voting categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers vote on whether captions are “Unfunny,” “Somewhat funny,” or “Funny,” then choose from finalists to select the ultimate winner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the three-tiered voting rubric used by The New Yorker’s caption contest; emphasizes democratic reader selection (rather than editorial or institutional filtering). Implied scoring note: most submissions—even top-rated—tend to receive many “Unfunny” ratings, indicating a high standard for getting broad laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity / difficulty of being humorous
rubrics_metrics.description: “Turns out that it’s extremely hard to be even moderately humorous.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A meta-criterion: good humor is uncommon and hard to achieve. Use this as a benchmark when judging: many attempts will fall short, so selectivity is required. Implies patience with submissions and high bar for what counts as funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human originality and nuance (A.I. limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the few things A.I. can’t do well is write a joke—a fact that we can all cling to...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality criterion: original, human-derived perspective and subtlety are central to effective jokes; mechanical or formulaic output (e.g., current A.I. jokes) will tend to fail. Reward improvisation, lived detail, and personal voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of three (comic structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentioned implicitly with: “Had to throw that in—rule of three.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural device: comedic lists or sequences often work best in threes (setup, buildup, punch). Use the three-part pattern to create expectation and subvert it on the third element. Applicable to captions, jokes, and satirical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical comedy / slapstick execution and prop use
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Enema Guy used the microphone stand and stool as props; Buster Keaton’s advice on the best type of pie to throw—doubled-up crust, uncooked filling, maybe some whipped cream on top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance for physical humor: effective use of simple props and precise execution matters. Specifics (e.g., pie construction) show that material choices and staging influence comedic payoff. Anti-pattern: sloppy or ill-considered prop use that undermines visual gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage presence / performer vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilton Als recounts Pryor walking onstage and announcing, “Hi. I’m Richard Pryor. Hope I’m funny.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance quality: a comic’s willingness to show vulnerability or low-stakes humility can be a comedic device that makes material land. Evaluate tone, timing, and the persona the performer projects; confidence plus self-deprecation often helps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taboo and transgressive content as comedic source (Freudian view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: “Jokes are our way of expressing otherwise taboo wishes (sleeping with your mother, killing your father, etc.).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content criterion: humor often derives from addressing taboo or repressed topics indirectly. When judging, consider whether transgressive material is handled with insight or merely shock; good taboo-based jokes reveal something about human nature rather than relying solely on offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific associative triggers (numbers, names, cultural details)
rubrics_metrics.description: References to purportedly funniest items—e.g., ‘the funniest number thirty-two (per Sid Caesar’s writers)’ and funniest names (per Melvin Helitzer) Gladys, Chuck, José, Hortense, and Lucky Pierre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational/technical note: certain sounds, names, or culturally resonant specifics are historically identified as reliably funny by some writers. Use phonetic, cultural, or absurd associative detail to amplify humor, but be mindful of dated or culturally narrow choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire targeted at institutions/places (local detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: cartoonists claim the F train is the best one to satirize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topical/local targeting: choosing a well-known institution/place (e.g., a subway line) provides shared context for satire. Effectiveness depends on audience familiarity; when judging, consider whether the target is recognizable and whether the satire adds fresh insight rather than lazy cliché.
